title: Authority grades — Divine equals Gospels; Apostolic equals Apostolic writings; Ecclesiastical equals canons
source_text: XIV. Caeterum omnibus istis traditionibus non omnino eandem authoritatem tribuunt. Et quidem traditiones illas quas divinas vocant, eandem vim habere volunt, quam divina praecepta & dogmata quae scripta sunt in Evangeliis. Et similiter traditionibus, quas Apostolicas dicunt, eandem authoritatem tribuendam esse statuunt, quam scriptis Apostolicis. Sed traditionibus Ecclesiasticis minorem aliquanto authoritatem deferunt, eam scilicet, quam habent Canones & Leges Ecclesiae scriptae.
pass_a_gloss: For the rest, they do not assign altogether the same authority to all these traditions. Indeed those they call Divine they will have to have the same force as the divine precepts and dogmas which are written in the Gospels. And likewise they decide that the same authority is to be given to those they call Apostolic as to the Apostolic writings. But to Ecclesiastical traditions they defer a somewhat lesser authority — namely that which the written Canons and Laws of the Church have.
pass_b_english: Authority is not equal across these kinds.
What they call Divine is given the same force as precepts and dogmas written in the Gospels.
What they call Apostolic is ranked with the Apostolic writings themselves.
Ecclesiastical traditions sit lower — on a level with the Church's written canons and laws.

lemmas.gloss: written Canons and Laws of the Church

choices.why: Marks graded authority; Ecclesiastical below Divine/Apostolic.
Assign authority downward to Ecclesiastical customs.
